system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2169-10-30 18:19:00 to 2169-11-08 14:18:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted after a fall that caused a right proximal tibia fracture. She underwent ORIF surgery and recovered well, with stable vital signs and controlled pain. Postoperatively, she developed mild wound redness attributed to hematoma, not infection, and was prescribed a short course of cephalexin as a precaution. Her chronic conditions, including HIV, hepatitis B and C, asthma, morbid obesity, and depression, remained stable. Blood pressure was managed with metoprolol, and psychiatric input led to an increase in duloxetine for mood and pain. She was transitioned to oral medications, prescribed enoxaparin for DVT prophylaxis, and discharged to extended care for rehabilitation with instructions to remain non-weight-bearing and complete her antibiotic and anticoagulant courses.
problems: Closed fracture of upper end of tibia alone
Viral hepatitis B without mention of hepatic coma, acute or unspecified, without mention of hepatitis delta
Unspecified viral hepatitis C without hepatic coma
Asymptomatic human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] infection status
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of ovary

radiology_notes.text:
SINGLE VIEW OF THE CHEST DATED ___

HISTORY:  ___ woman with "outside" PICC placement; evaluate position.

FINDINGS:  Single bedside AP examination labeled "upright" is compared with
supine examination of ___, as well as study obtained the preceding day.  No
PICC or other central venous catheter is identified.  The lungs are
well-inflated and clear.  The cardiomediastinal silhouette and pulmonary
vessels are within normal limits and there is no pleural effusion.  Again
demonstrated is the sideplate with threaded cortical screw device transfixing
an apparently healed fracture of the right humeral surgical neck, incompletely
imaged.  The regional skeleton is otherwise grossly unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:  

1.  PICC, purportedly placed at outside hospital is not identified; this
should be correlated with physical examination.

2.  No acute cardiopulmonary process.

COMMENT:  Dr. ___ was notified with these findings, in the OR, at 1110H,
___.

INDICATION:  Patient is a ___ female with PICC line.  Unable to place
centrally.

RADIOLOGISTS:  Drs. ___, and ___ performed the procedure. Dr.
___ Attending ___, reviewed this exam.

The procedure was explained to the patient.  A timeout was performed.  Note
that, upon review of ___ medical record, patient stated to have
anaphylactic reaction to iodinated contrast.

Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, a guide wire was advanced
through the indwelling left arm PICC, and subsequently further attempts to
pass the wire centrally were unsuccessful.  Contrast was deferred secondary to
known contrast allergy.  Discussion was performed with the primary team, who
stated midline was okay to use.  Subsequently, a new single lumen midline
measuring 38 cm in length was then placed through a peel-away sheath with its
tip positioned within the left axillary vein under fluoroscopic guidance.
Position of the catheter was confirmed by a fluoroscopic spot film of the
chest.  The peel-away sheath and guide wire were then removed.  The catheter
was secured to the skin, flushed, and sterile dressing was applied.  Note
that, 9 cm of catheter was left external to the patient.  The patient
tolerated the procedure well.  There were no immediate complications.

IMPRESSION:  Uncomplicated fluoroscopic-guided successful PICC line exchange
to a new single lumen midline, with final internal length of 29 cm.  The tip
is positioned within the left axillary vein.  The line is ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you came in because of drainage from your right leg wound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started a few days ago—yellowish and a little smelly. I was worried it might be infected again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. You had surgery on that leg not long ago, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about two months ago for a fracture. They fixed it with hardware. I’ve been in rehab since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check the wound and likely take you to surgery tomorrow to clean it out. We’ll also get cultures to see if there’s an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another surgery? I’m nervous about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a minor procedure—just to irrigate and debride the area. We’ll close it afterward. It’s important to prevent the infection from spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds better. What about my PICC line? It’s been in since rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a chest X-ray, and we couldn’t see the tip. It might not be in the right place. We’ll likely replace it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that could happen. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not immediately, but we need reliable IV access for antibiotics. We’ll place a new one under imaging guidance to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re prepping you for surgery today. We’ll clean out the wound and close it. Then we’ll place a new PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. Will I be able to eat afterward?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be NPO until we confirm you’re stable. Then we’ll start with clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you did well in surgery. We cleaned out the wound and closed it. Cultures were taken—we’ll know more in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infected? The pain is better, but I’m still worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We suspect infection, so we’ve started antibiotics—vancomycin and meropenem—just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember I’m allergic to vancomycin. I get a rash and flushing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for reminding me. We’ll switch you to daptomycin instead. I’ll update your allergy in the chart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good, I appreciate that. What about the PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s in place now—new one, tip in the axillary vein. It’s working well for your antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The culture came back. You have Morganella morganii and some Enterococcus. That confirms the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I’ve never heard of that bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a type of gram-negative bacteria. Your antibiotics—daptomycin and meropenem—cover it well. You’re on the right treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m glad we caught it early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed some new drainage from the wound this morning. We might need to go back to the OR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? Is it not healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes wounds like this need more than one cleaning. We’ll place a VAC—vacuum-assisted closure—to help it heal from the inside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s a VAC? Does it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a sponge with suction. It helps remove fluid and pull the wound together. We’ll numb the area before placing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well in surgery yesterday. The VAC is working. We’ll change it every few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels tight, but not painful. How long will I need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually a week or two. We’ll monitor healing and switch to regular dressings when ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics? How long will I be on IVs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Six weeks total. You’ll go home with the PICC line and continue meropenem through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Six weeks? That’s a long time. Can I manage that at rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the facility is set up for IV antibiotics. A nurse will help you each time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We changed the VAC today. The wound looks much better—good granulation tissue, no pus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does this mean I’m healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. We’ll keep the VAC for a few more days, then switch to regular care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood clots? I’m still on lovenox and warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your DVT is still there. Your INR is a bit low, so we’re keeping both for now. Once your INR reaches the goal, you’ll stop lovenox.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How often will they check my INR?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Daily for now, then weekly once it’s stable. The rehab team will handle that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs look good—white count is normal, CRP is coming down. Blood cultures are negative—no sign the infection spread.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Can I start moving more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can work with physical therapy, but still no weight on that leg. Focus on range of motion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll keep doing my exercises.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. The wound is stable, and you’re doing well on antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you get a fever, increased redness, or more drainage. Keep the VAC on and change it every three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain meds? I’m on hydromorphone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use them as needed, but try to wean. Don’t drive or operate machinery while on them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my HIV meds? I’ve been taking them every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking them exactly as before. They’re important for your immune system, especially now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for making sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go. Your wound looks great—no redness, VAC is working, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. It’s been a long week, but I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Continue all meds, especially antibiotics for six weeks and anticoagulants as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll get weekly labs and follow up with my doctors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The rehab team will coordinate everything. Call us if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate all your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I watch for constipation? I’m on methadone and pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. Keep using your stool softeners and senna as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The transport team will take you to rehab shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care and keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch with your rehab team to ensure smooth care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. I feel confident going back now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Keep healing and stay in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Have a safe transfer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. We’ll talk soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well and keep up with your care plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for a right tibial wound infection following prior ORIF surgery. She underwent irrigation and debridement with primary closure, but due to persistent drainage, a second surgery was performed to place a VAC. Cultures grew Morganella morganii and Enterococcus, prompting antibiotic therapy with meropenem and daptomycin after an adverse reaction to vancomycin. A non-functional PICC line was replaced with a new midline catheter. The wound showed progressive healing with granulation tissue, and the patient remained afebrile and stable. She was anticoagulated for a known DVT, with warfarin dosing adjusted to reach therapeutic INR. She was discharged to extended care on a six-week course of IV meropenem, with instructions for VAC changes, anticoagulation management, and close monitoring for infection recurrence.
